title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization

pages.title: The question vanilla RAG can't answer
pages.subtitle: Local lookups vs. global sensemaking

blocks.html: Imagine you have a 1-million-token pile of text — a year of podcast transcripts, or every news article about a company — and someone asks: "What are the main themes in this corpus?" Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is hopeless here. RAG works by finding the few chunks of text most similar to your question and stuffing them into the prompt. That is perfect when the answer lives in one place ("What was the Q3 revenue?"), but a question about themes has no single home — the answer is spread across the entire dataset. There is nothing specific to retrieve.

The paper calls these query-focused summarization (QFS) or global sensemaking questions. They ask you to connect the dots across thousands of documents at once. You can't retrieve your way to that answer — and you can't fit 1M tokens in a context window either. This is the gap GraphRAG fills.
We propose a Graph RAG approach to question answering over private text corpora that scales with both the generality of user questions and the quantity of source text to be indexed.

The core idea, in one sentence: pre-compute structure once, so global questions become cheap at query time. GraphRAG uses an LLM to read the whole corpus and build a knowledge graph of entities and relationships. It then finds tightly-connected communities in that graph and writes a summary of each community ahead of time. When a global question arrives, every community summary takes a stab at it in parallel, and the partial answers are merged into one. The graph is the index; the community summaries are the pre-chewed answers.

The headline result: on two ~1M-token datasets, GraphRAG substantially beat a conventional vector-search RAG baseline on the comprehensiveness and diversity of generated answers, as judged head-to-head by an LLM. And its most compressed variant matched a brute-force "summarize all the source text" approach while using as little as 2–3% of the tokens.

Authored by a Microsoft Research team (Darren Edge, Ha Trinh, and colleagues), the open-source graphrag release made this one of the most influential RAG papers of 2024 — it reframed RAG from "find the relevant chunk" to "understand the whole corpus."

pages.title: Why retrieval breaks on global questions
pages.subtitle: Two failed alternatives, and the gap between them

blocks.html: To see why a new method is needed, picture the two obvious things you could try instead — and why each one fails.

Embed every chunk, embed the question, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks, answer from those. This is the dominant RAG recipe and it is excellent for local questions where the answer text exists somewhere specific. But ask "what are the top 5 themes?" and the retriever has no anchor — a theme isn't a phrase you can match. You get a handful of arbitrary chunks and a shallow, partial answer that misses most of the corpus. The paper's own results later show vector RAG (condition SS) losing on comprehensiveness 72–83% of the time.

If the answer is everywhere, just feed the LLM all the text and ask it to summarize. With modern long-context models you can even do this in a map-reduce loop: summarize each chunk, then summarize the summaries. This actually works for quality — it's the paper's TS (source-text summarization) condition and it's strong. The problem is cost: you pay to read every token of every source chunk, for every query. On 1M tokens that is enormous and it does not scale to repeated questions.

GraphRAG threads the needle: get the broad coverage of "summarize everything" but pay for reading the corpus once, up front, not per query. The trick is to do the expensive reading at index time and store the result as a structure you can query cheaply.
Naive RAG fails on global questions such as “What are the main themes in the dataset?”, since this is inherently a query-focused summarization (QFS) task, rather than an explicit retrieval task.

The other ingredient is an old graph-theory observation: real-world entity graphs have community structure — dense clusters of related nodes with sparse links between clusters. Each community is a natural "theme" the corpus is talking about. If you summarize communities, you've effectively pre-computed the answer to "what are the themes?" before anyone asks.

pages.title: From text chunks to a knowledge graph
pages.subtitle: Step 1–2 of the indexing pipeline

blocks.html: GraphRAG's pipeline has two halves. Index time (done once): chunk → extract graph → detect communities → summarize communities. Query time (done per question): map every relevant community summary onto the question, then reduce the partials into one answer. This page covers the first two index-time steps; the next page covers the rest. We'll follow the source text all the way to a queryable structure.

Split the corpus into chunks of a fixed size. The size is a real trade-off. The paper tests this directly: with 600-token chunks the extractor found nearly 2× as many entity references as with 2400-token chunks on the same text (their Figure 2 finds roughly 2x more entities at 600 vs 2400 tokens). Why? An LLM asked to extract entities from a long chunk gets lazy and misses things; shorter chunks force more careful reads. But shorter chunks mean more LLM calls and more cost. The paper uses 600 tokens as the sweet spot.

For each chunk, a single LLM prompt does the heavy lifting. It pulls out entities (people, places, organizations — each with a name, type, and a short generated description) and relationships (which entities are connected, plus a description of how). It also extracts claims — factual statements about entities. This is the step that turns flat prose into structured nodes and edges.

Concretely, a chunk mentioning "NeoChip's CTO, Maria Santos, announced the acquisition of Verdyn Systems" yields nodes Maria Santos (person), NeoChip (org), Verdyn Systems (org), and edges Maria Santos —CTO of→ NeoChip and NeoChip —acquired→ Verdyn Systems. The same entity surfaces in many chunks; GraphRAG collects all the descriptions per entity and lets the LLM summarize them into one, so a node carries everything the corpus knows about it.

blocks.tex: G = (V, E), \quad v \in V \text{ an entity}, \quad (u, v) \in E \text{ a relationship}

blocks.html: Reading it term by term: $G$ is the resulting knowledge graph. $V$ is the set of nodes, one per distinct entity $v$ (deduplicated across all chunks). $E$ is the set of edges; an edge $(u, v)$ means entities $u$ and $v$ co-occur in some relationship. In practice edges carry a weight — the number of source chunks that detected that relationship — so a link mentioned 50 times is heavier than one mentioned once, which matters for the clustering step next.

Why a graph and not a vector store? A vector store knows that two chunks are similar; it has no idea that two entities are connected. Global sensemaking is about connections — who relates to whom, which topics cluster — so an explicit graph is the natural substrate. It's also why GraphRAG can answer "how are X and Y related?" questions vanilla RAG can't reach.

pages.title: Communities and their summaries
pages.subtitle: Step 3–4: Leiden clustering and hierarchical summaries

blocks.html: We now have a graph with possibly millions of edges. Step 3 carves it into communities — groups of entities that talk to each other far more than to the rest of the graph. Each community is, in effect, a topic the corpus keeps circling back to. Step 4 writes a report-style summary of each one. These summaries are the pre-computed global knowledge.

The paper uses the Leiden algorithm (Traag et al., 2019), the modern fix to the older Louvain method, because it is fast on large graphs and — crucially — produces a hierarchy. At the top level the graph splits into a few big communities; each of those splits into sub-communities; and so on down to small, tightly-knit groups. This gives a tree of granularity.
Community detection optimizes modularity, the gap between observed within-cluster edges and what you'd expect by chance:

Term by term: $Q$ is modularity, a single number measuring how good a clustering is (higher = denser communities). $A_{ij}$ is the weight of the edge between nodes $i$ and $j$ (0 if none). $k_i$ is the degree of node $i$ (sum of its edge weights), so $\frac{k_i k_j}{2m}$ is the edge weight you'd expect between $i$ and $j$ if edges were random. $m$ is the total edge weight in the graph; the $\frac{1}{2m}$ normalizes. $\delta(c_i, c_j)$ is the Kronecker delta — it equals $1$ when $i$ and $j$ are in the same community $c$ and $0$ otherwise, so the sum only counts within-community edges. Leiden searches partitions to maximize $Q$. (This is the standard objective Leiden optimizes; the paper invokes Leiden rather than re-deriving it.)

For a leaf community, GraphRAG prioritizes its element summaries (the most-connected nodes, their strongest edges, and associated claims) and packs as many as fit into one LLM prompt, which writes a stand-alone report. For a higher-level community that is too big to fit, it doesn't re-read the raw text — it substitutes the already-written sub-community summaries for the longest elements, recursively. The hierarchy is summarized from the leaves up.

The payoff is a set of summaries at every level of granularity. The paper names these levels C0 (root — a few broad summaries), C1, C2, and C3 (leaf — many fine-grained summaries). Coarse levels are cheap and give the big picture; fine levels are richer but cost more tokens. The same corpus is now queryable at whichever zoom level suits the question — a knob vanilla RAG simply doesn't have.

pages.title: Answering a global query: map-reduce
pages.subtitle: Step 5: from community summaries to one answer

blocks.html: Now a user asks a global question. There is no retrieval over source text — instead GraphRAG runs a map-reduce over community summaries at a chosen level (say C1). The whole point of all that index-time work was to make this step cheap and parallel.

blocks.text: Map: every community answers in parallel

blocks.html: Shuffle the community summaries and pack them into context-window-sized batches (shuffling avoids concentrating related info in one prompt). For each batch, the LLM produces a list of partial answers — and, critically, rates each partial with a helpfulness score from 0 to 100 for how much it actually addresses the question. Partials scored 0 are discarded.

Reading it term by term: $q$ is the user's question. $\text{batch}_i$ is the $i$-th bundle of community summaries that fit in one prompt. $a_i$ is the partial answer the LLM generates from that batch. $s_i \in [0, 100]$ is the helpfulness score the LLM assigns to its own partial — a self-rated relevance signal. Keeping only $s_i > 0$ throws away batches that had nothing useful to say about $q$.

Sort the surviving partials by score, highest first, and add them to a final context window until it's full. The LLM reads this curated, ranked set of partial answers and writes the single global answer the user sees. The score-sort matters: the most relevant community contributions land in the final prompt; the marginal ones get dropped if space runs out.

Why this beats stuffing everything into one prompt: a million tokens of summaries won't fit, and even if they did, the model would drown. Map-reduce lets every community weigh in on the question (broad coverage → high comprehensiveness and diversity) while the helpfulness score keeps the final answer focused (relevance → not just a data dump). It's the mechanism that turns "many local views" into one global answer — the paper's title, literally.

Concrete example: ask "what are the main themes?" over the podcast corpus. Community A (about AI regulation) returns "regulatory uncertainty is a recurring concern" with score 95; community B (about chip supply chains) returns a supply-shock theme with score 88; a community about studio mic setups returns score 0 and is dropped. The reduce step weaves the high scorers into a coherent thematic overview — something no single retrieved chunk could ever produce.

pages.title: Does it actually answer global questions better?
pages.subtitle: Head-to-head LLM evaluation on two 1M-token corpora

blocks.html: There's no gold-standard "correct" answer to "what are the themes?", so the paper can't score against a reference. Instead it runs a head-to-head LLM judge: for each question, the judge sees two answers (from two methods) side by side and picks a winner, repeated to get a win-rate percentage. This is a now-standard way to evaluate open-ended generation.

items: Two datasets, each ~1 million tokens: podcast transcripts (~1669 chunks at 600 tokens) and news articles (~3197 chunks).
Conditions: C0–C3 = GraphRAG at root/intermediate/low/leaf community levels; TS = map-reduce summarization over the raw source text; SS = conventional vector-search RAG (the baseline to beat).
Questions were LLM-generated to be genuinely global — by describing the corpus to an LLM and asking for high-level sensemaking questions a user might pose.

Four metrics, each judged head-to-head: Comprehensiveness (covers all aspects?), Diversity (varied perspectives?), Empowerment (helps the reader reach an informed judgment?), and Directness (specific and to the point?).

blocks.html: Against the vector-RAG baseline (SS), GraphRAG won decisively on the two metrics that matter most for sensemaking. The win rates for GraphRAG over SS:

headers: GraphRAG win rate vs. vector RAG (SS)

blocks.html: The pattern is intuitive. GraphRAG pulls in every community's view, so its answers are broader (comprehensiveness) and pull in more distinct angles (diversity). Vector RAG retrieves a few tight chunks, so it wins on directness — it's concise because it's narrow. For global sensemaking, breadth is exactly what you want, and that's the win GraphRAG claims.
Both global approaches outperformed the naïve RAG baseline (SS) in comprehensiveness and diversity... global approaches consistently outperformed the naïve RAG approach on both datasets.

pages.title: The efficiency win: matching brute force at a fraction of the cost
pages.subtitle: Why the root level (C0) is the punchline

blocks.html: Beating vector RAG is nice, but the real surprise is GraphRAG vs. the strong baseline — TS, which reads and summarizes all the source text. TS is expensive but thorough, so matching it cheaply is the prize.

The standout is the root level, C0: just a handful of top-level community summaries. C0 produced answers competitive with the much costlier TS and the lower GraphRAG levels on comprehensiveness and diversity — while using dramatically fewer tokens.

The paper reports that root-level community summaries required as little as 2–3% of the context tokens of the source-text approach while remaining competitive on quality. That is the whole thesis paying off: because the corpus was digested into community summaries once, a global query touches only a tiny, pre-distilled slice of text yet still reflects the whole dataset.

There's also a clean granularity dial. Lower levels (C2/C3) give richer, more detailed answers but cost more tokens; the root level (C0) is the efficient default. You pick the level to match how much depth the question deserves — a control surface that flat vector RAG simply doesn't offer.

What this buys in practice: for a corpus that gets queried repeatedly, you pay the expensive LLM-extraction bill once at index time, then serve global questions for the token cost of a few summaries. That cost amortization is what makes "ask global questions over a private corpus" economically viable at all.

pages.title: Why GraphRAG mattered
pages.subtitle: Impact, trade-offs, and what it changed

blocks.html: GraphRAG reframed what RAG is for. Before it, RAG meant "retrieve the relevant chunk." GraphRAG showed that by spending LLM effort at index time to build structure, you can answer a whole class of questions — global, thematic, sensemaking questions — that retrieval alone cannot touch. From local to global is the literal contribution: turning many local entity facts into a global understanding.

GraphRAG is not free. It front-loads cost: an LLM must read the entire corpus to extract entities, relationships, and write community summaries before you can ask a single question. That index is also stale when the corpus changes (though the hierarchy makes incremental updates feasible). The bet is that for a corpus queried many times, paying once up front and then answering global questions for the cost of a few summaries is a clear win — and the 2–3%-of-tokens result is the evidence.

When is it not worth it? For purely local lookups ("what did the report say about X?"), plain vector RAG is cheaper and more direct — and the paper's own directness numbers admit as much. GraphRAG earns its keep specifically on whole-corpus questions.

blocks.text: How it connects to the landscape

items: It builds on classic RAG (Lewis et al., 2020) but replaces the vector index with an LLM-built knowledge graph — reviving structured knowledge in the LLM era.
It leans on decades of graph community detection (Louvain → Leiden, Traag et al. 2019), applying modularity-based clustering to an LLM-extracted graph.
It echoes map-reduce summarization (the TS baseline) but pre-computes the per-region summaries, decoupling the expensive read from the per-query cost.
The LLM-as-judge head-to-head evaluation reflects the same shift toward model-graded open-ended generation seen across 2023–2024 LLM research.

blocks.html: Microsoft Research open-sourced the implementation as the graphrag package, which spread quickly and spawned a wave of follow-ups (LightRAG, GraphReader, and many "agentic" and hybrid graph-plus-vector retrieval systems). The lasting lesson: the right pre-computed structure can answer questions that no amount of clever retrieval can — spend the LLM tokens building understanding once, and global sensemaking becomes cheap forever after.
